newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea unveils moves to combat trade deficit.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea unveils moves to combat trade deficit.

text.p: South Korea, alarmed by a ballooning trade deficit, announced a series of measures on Tuesday to control prices and spending and boost corporate competitiveness.

A statement from the Ministry of Finance and Economy said South Korea would focus on price stability to improve the overall health of the economy and bring down a current account deficit that is hitting record highs.

The government would try to cut public utility charges by 5-10 percent next year, freeze the pay of public servants except for police and teachers and keep overall wage increases within single digits.
To help the corporate sector, the government would relax controls on overseas borrowing, a move that would bring down domestic interest rates, the statement said.
"Without price stability it is impossible to strengthen competitiveness," the statement said.

However, the government was not proposing excessive belt-tightening that could hit small- and medium-sized companies. Instead, it would promote savings, the statement said, repeating an earlier announcement of a tax break on three-year household bank savings.
Tax incentives also would be offered on savings accounts with securities houses for stock market investment.
South Korea's August trade deficit hit a record $2.9 billion against a year earlier shortfall of $901 million.
"We are not going to rely on short-term, quick-fix policies to redress current problems because these would worsen the situation," the statement said.
The statement gave no details on how the measures to cut utility charges and freeze pay would be implemented.

It said the government would crack down on excessive consumption by, for instance, running tax audits on individuals and companies suspected of lavish spending. Corporate entertainment expenses would be monitored.
"Soaring consumption is now becoming a headache for the country's economy," the statement said.
Foreigners would be allowed direct access to the over-the-counter stock market, the statement said. Currently, they can invest only through instiutionally-managed funds.

The statement said high wages and interest rates and a weak financial structure was hurting the ecnonomy. Average bank interest rates for corporate borrowers were 13.8 percent last year, compared with three percent in Japan.
It said the government would invest more in infrastructure to bring down transport and distribution costs, which eat up about 17 percent of total sales.

South Korea's current account deficit during the fist seven months of this year rose to a record high of $11.66 billion, compared with $6.5 billion a year earlier, according to the central Bank of Korea.
Gross domestic product growth slowed to a real 7.2 percent in the first half of this year, against growth of 9.8 percent a year before.
The consumer price index, South Korea's leading inflation indicator, rose a year-on-year 5.3 percent in August, up from a 3.5 percent rise a year ago.
